hints: Reaching the end tile is not enough: the route must cover every non-wall tile. What number could you track during the walk to know whether you have covered everything?
Backtracking DFS from the start tile. Count the non-wall tiles first, then carry how many are still unvisited; mark tiles as walls while they are on the current path.

1. Count all non-wall tiles (start and end included) and find the start.
  2. DFS(cell, left): if this is the end tile, return 1 when left == 1, else 0.
  3. Mark the cell as -1.
  4. Add up DFS on each in-bounds, non-wall neighbour with left − 1.
  5. Restore the cell and return the total.

approaches.name: Backtracking DFS
approaches.idea: Explore every simple path from the start, counting only those that reach the end after visiting every free tile. The grid has at most 20 cells, so this is fast enough.

approaches.name: Alternative: bitmask DP
approaches.idea: Memoize on (current tile, visited mask). It caps the work but needs 2<sup>N</sup>·N states, which is not needed at this size.

explain: In the 3×3 sample all 9 tiles are free, so the robot must make 8 moves and finish on the end tile in the bottom-right. Exactly 2 routes work: one snakes row by row and the other snakes column by column. Every other walk either gets stuck or reaches the end too early, when left is still above 1, and scores 0. Marking path tiles as -1 during the DFS and restoring them afterwards stops revisits without extra memory. In the second sample both neighbours of the start lead straight to the end tile after only 3 tiles, so no route covers all four and the answer is 0.
recognize: Count paths that must visit every free cell exactly once on a tiny grid → backtracking DFS with a 'cells left' counter.
